FALSIFIABLE
Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample.
Let $T_2,\ldots,T_n$ be a collection of trees such that $T_k$ has $k$ vertices. Can we always write $K_n$ as the edge disjoint union of the $T_k$?
#743: [Er81]
graph theory
A conjecture of Gyárfás, known as the tree packing conjecture.
Gyárfás and Lehel [GyLe78] proved that this holds if all but at most $2$ of the trees are stars, or if all the trees are stars or paths. Fishburn [Fi83] proved this for $n\leq 9$. Bollobás [Bo83] proved that the smallest $\lfloor n/\sqrt{2}\rfloor$ many trees can always be packed greedily into $K_n$.
Joos, Kim, Kühn, and Osthus [JKKO19] proved that this conjecture holds when the trees have bounded maximum degree. Allen, Böttcher, Clemens, Hladky, Piguet, and Taraz [ABCHPT21] proved that this conjecture holds when all the trees have maximum degree $\leq c\frac{n}{\log n}$ for some constant $c>0$.
Janzer and Montgomery [JaMo24] have proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that the largest $cn$ trees can be packed into $K_n$.
Additional thanks to: Zach Hunter

 Exhaustive verification at $n = 12$. Following up on my note about [GuMa90]: I have now checked the conjecture for $n = 12$, the first case not covered by a published exhaustive computation. All sequences $(T_2, \dots, T_{12})$ with $|T_k| = k$ pack into $K_{12}$.
Method: fix the embedding of $T_{12}$ (all are equivalent under $S_{12}$), place trees largest first, and memoise the residual graph on its isomorphism class (nauty canonical form) together with the set of prefix answers. The 551 choices of $T_{12}$ are independent jobs; each ran with its own memo table, 239 on an Apple M-series laptop and 312 on two 16-vCPU cloud machines, about 220 core-hours in total (the cloud vCPUs were roughly 4x slower per job than the laptop cores). The largest job needed 6.3 million memoised classes.
What was checked and what was not, so nobody has to take my word for more than I can back up:
- $n \le 11$ was re-derived by the same code as a regression; $n = 11$ (290 CPU-seconds) agrees with [GuMa90].
- A second implementation written from scratch (tree generation from Prüfer sequences, its own canonical form, no shared code) agrees with the first for $n = 4, \dots, 9$. It has not been run at $n = 10, 11, 12$.
- 8 of the 551 jobs at $n = 12$ were computed twice, on the laptop and in the cloud, with identical outcomes and identical family counts.
- So $n = 12$ rests on one implementation, cross-checked against a second one only up to $n = 9$. I would not call it independently verified until someone else's code reproduces it.
Per-job JSON summaries (state counts, family counts, CPU time), both implementations and a one-line command to reproduce any single job: github.com/pawelkwaczynski/erdos743. Each job takes between 4 minutes and 1.3 hours on one core, so the whole thing is reproducible on a laptop over a few days.

 A reference that seems to be missing from the summary above: Fishburn's $n \leq 9$ is not the frontier of exhaustive verification. David R. Guichard and John D. Massman, A note on packing complete graphs with trees, J. Combin. Math. Combin. Comput. 8 (1990), 123-126, write in the abstract: "Using a computer, we have shown that the conjecture is true through $n = 11$, but also that an approach suggested by Fishburn is unlikely to work in general." So the $n = 10$ computation posted above is an independent re-verification of a 1990 result, and the first case not covered by a published exhaustive check is $n = 12$. It would be worth adding [GuMa90] to the page next to [Fi83].

 Verification at $n = 10$.
Hi I worked on this problem with the help of Opus 5 on xhigh effort, and I believe the conjecture holds for $n = 10$: all $45{,}376{,}056$ sequences $(T_2, \dots, T_{10})$ with $|T_k| = k$ decompose $K_{10}$ perfectly. That extends Fishburn's $n \le 9$ by one.
The method is straightforward. All embeddings of $T_{10}$ are equivalent under $\operatorname{Aut}(K_{10}) = S_{10}$, so one is fixed and never branched on; trees go in largest-first; and the residual graph is memoised on its isomorphism class with a bitset of all prefix answers. $108{,}688{,}803$ level-6 calls collapse onto $106{,}123$ classes, and the whole thing runs in about $150$ seconds on one core.
Most of the work went into not believing it, since "everything packs" is exactly what a bug produces. Every one of the $121{,}628{,}509$ memo hits in the actual run was re-checked against an independently written isomorphism test (backtracking bijection, no canonical form) — 0 failures. A differential test against clean-room brute force compared $47{,}520$ bits including 222 genuine zeros — 0 mismatches. The canonical form was validated exhaustively over all $2^{28}$ graphs on 8 vertices, giving 12,346 classes, the known count, and again at $n = 10$ for $m \le 7$. $n \le 9$ was re-derived as a regression, and $40{,}098$ explicit packings were checked by separate code.
To be clear about $n = 11$: I only decided restricted subfamilies there, $91{,}032$ exhaustively and $33{,}425$ certified, out of roughly $1.07 \times 10^{10}$. That is not a decision about $n = 11$.
Given the discussion above about arXiv:2410.13840, I should say this is offered as an independent verification at one value of $n$ and not as a novelty claim — if that preprint is right then it subsumes this entirely, and as zach hunter and Nat Sothanaphan note, that is not currently settled either way.
Code, certificates and reproduction instructions: github.com/RajveerKapoor/erdos-work (743/).

 Claimed proof (preprint):
Parikshit Chalise, Antwan Clark, and Edinah K. Gnang posted “A Proof of the Tree Packing Conjecture” (arXiv:2410.13840; v2 dated 23 Oct 2024), which claims to prove Gyárfás’ Tree Packing Conjecture for all $n$.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13840
High-level outline (as stated by the authors):
The paper introduces a reformulation of tree packing into $K_n$ via “augmented functional trees” and reduces the existence of an edge-disjoint packing of $(T_2,\dots,T_n)$ into $K_n$ to a “complete labeling” problem.
They define a “tree packing polynomial certificate” $P_g(X,y)=V(X)E_g(X,y)$ and (Proposition 3.4) relate existence of a complete labeling to a non-vanishing condition for a canonical representative of $P_g$.
A key step is the “Composition Lemma” (Lemma 3.10), asserting that the relevant non-vanishing property is preserved under a local composition operation; iterating this is used to reduce general instances to a star-based instance, yielding Theorem 1.9 and the main claimed result.
Status note:
This is a preprint; I have not found a refereed journal version or a widely circulated independent verification. There is community discussion about related “composition lemma” approaches here:
https://mathoverflow.net/questions/482509/claimed-proofs-of-graph-labelling-conjectures
Suggestion for this page:
It may be useful to add arXiv:2410.13840 as a reference (possibly marked “claimed proof / pending verification”), and update the open/solved status if/when a vetted confirmation appears.
